items.title: Leaning on the Machine: Does Relying on AI for Everyday Tasks Build an Emotional Bond? Evidence from University Students
items.abstract: Plenty of students now ask AI to explain a topic, check an essay, or settle a decision. But does depending on AI for tasks like these also tie them to it emotionally? This study looked at whether reliance on AI predicts Human–AI relationship among university students. We used a cross-sectional survey design and collected data from 300 students (158 men, 142 women) through convenient sampling. Reliance was measured with the Reliance on Artificial Intelligence Scale (RAI-15; Yap et al., 2023) and the Human–AI relationship with the Experiences in Human–AI Relationships Scale (EHARS; Yang & Oshio, 2025). Reliability was acceptable to good (α = .76 and .83). Reliance on AI was positively correlated with Human–AI relationship (r = .23, p < .001) and was a significant but modest predictor of it, explaining about 5% of the variance. Men reported higher reliance on AI (d = 0.32) and a stronger Human–AI relationship (d = 0.34) than women. The results suggest that using and depending on AI for practical purposes is linked to an emotional bond with it, though only weakly. We discuss what this means for AI literacy and for future research in Pakistan.

items.title: Learning Global Probabilistic Explanations
items.abstract: Interpreting the predictions of complex black-box classifiers remains a central challenge in explainable artificial intelligence. While local explanations clarify individual predictions, there is a significant need for global probabilistic explanations that capture a model's overall behavior across the input distribution. Such an explanation is a small subset $K$ of features, whose relevance is measured by the expected probability, over a random input $\mathbf x$, that the classifier assigns the same label to $\mathbf x$ and to a random input agreeing with $\mathbf x$ on $K$. In this study, we investigate the task of identifying maximally relevant global explanations under a cardinality constraint, focusing on product distributions with full support on discrete feature spaces. We introduce a spectral explainer that leverages membership queries to the black-box classifier and employs Fourier-analytic, junta-learning methods to produce probably approximately correct (PAC) explanations. Our algorithm is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the explanation size limit, maximum feature cardinality, and desired accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the theoretical guarantees and show that the spectral explainer outperforms a greedy baseline as the explanation size increases.

items.title: Managing Verification Debt: A Framework for Responsible Human-AI Research Partnerships
items.abstract: Conversation with generative artificial intelligence (AI) can quickly turn a tentative scientific question into the outline of a research programme. Although this capability can accelerate research, it also places two closely related pressures on human intelligence: 1) temporal asymmetry between rapid AI generation and slower expert evaluation, and 2) a cognitive gap between the available effort, expertise, attention and capacity to assess AI outputs. When unexamined AI contributions are carried into subsequent claims or decisions, these pressures produce verification debt: validation work that remains outstanding before a contribution can be relied upon. If left unresolved, this debt can undermine responsible AI in research, understood here as the transparent and traceable use of AI under effective human oversight and accountability. This commentary argues that responsible human--AI research partnerships therefore require a disciplined method for managing verification debt, not better prompting alone. We propose a shared topology of the research programme: a structured representation that connects questions, claims, assumptions, sources, tests and decisions while recording their provenance, dependencies and verification status. The topology makes unresolved debt visible, enables corrections to propagate through dependent claims and requires consequential contributions to be examined at decision gates before research proceeds. We consider its application in two-way partnerships and supervised partnerships that extend from doctoral research to multi-way research teams, and examine its implications for scholarly assessment, peer review and empirical evaluation.

items.title: Mental Skills Attenuate the Impact of Performance Anxiety on Self-Perceived Performance Quality in Professional Musicians
items.abstract: Human performance in the performing arts is a complex, multifaceted experience intertwining technical proficiency, artistic expression, and psychological resilience to anxiety and stress. One key factor influencing a musician’s success and well-being is self-perceived performance quality (SPPQ), which plays a vital role in motivation, confidence, and career longevity. Sport psychology frameworks such as S.F.E.R.A. (Synchrony, Force/Strength, Energy, Rhythm, Activation) support optimal performance by monitoring and improving related mental factors. This study investigated the relationships among SPPQ, music performance anxiety (MPA), and mental skills as assessed by the SFERA model in professional musicians. Eighty-two participants (53% females) completed an online survey including the SFERA questionnaire and the Kenny Music Performance Anxiety Inventory (K-MPAI). We found significant negative correlations between SPPQ and MPA, and significant positive correlations between SPPQ and SFERA (total and subfactor scores). “Force” (i.e., strength of personal resources), proximal somatic anxiety, memory issues, and biological vulnerability emerged as the strongest predictors of SPPQ in the variable importance analysis. In other words, musicians with higher anxiety tended to report lower SPPQ and lower SFERA mental skills. Further mediation analysis showed that SFERA scores mediated approximately 60% (proportion mediated = 0.618, 95% confidence interval [0.148, 1.331]) of the association between MPA and SPPQ. These findings underscore the applicability of sport-based mental skills models to music contexts and highlight the potential protective role of mental skills in mitigating the impact of performance anxiety on performers’ self-perceived quality.

items.title: Multi-scale approach for the characterization of the thermal degradation of poly(lactic acid)
items.abstract: In recent years, the increased use of biodegradable materials has raised several concerns regarding their flammability and thermal reactivity when exposed to intense heat radiation from nearby fires. Among others, Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is one of the most commercially successful biodegradable polymers in several applications and industrial sectors such as packaging, consumer goods, and automotive components. This work presents a multi-scale experimental investigation of PLA degradation, combining small-scale analyses (i.e., thermogravimetric analysis coupled with FTIR and mass spectrometry) with bench-scale testing (i.e., cone calorimetry). The integration of these techniques, supported by temperature distribution measurements, enables the identification of the sequential physical and chemical phenomena controlling ignition, volatilisation, and combustion, providing a comprehensive evaluation of the fire response of the material across different conditions. Small scale tests have identified a decomposition temperature of ∼250 °C either in nitrogen or air, indicating a limited contribution of heterogeneous reactions within the decomposition process. At bench scale, a threshold value of 15 kW/m 2 was identified as the maximum external heat flux to guarantee the absence of sustained ignition or self-sustained decomposition. The formation of acetic acid was identified as a key intermediate, with apparent flame spread velocities (S u,app ) ranging from 0.0011 to 0.0018 cm/s, indicating gas-phase reactions occur almost instantaneously once volatiles are released. The characteristic times of the key thermal phenomena were quantified through combined analysis of heat release profiles, evolved gases, and temperature gradients, revealing that the temporal evolution of melting, liquid heating, and volatilisation occurs over comparable time scales. This approach advances the mechanistic understanding of bio-based polymer combustion and provides valuable tools for the design of safer materials in fire-sensitive industrial applications.

items.title: PROMOÇÃO DA SAÚDE MENTAL E PREVENÇÃO DA SÍNDROME DE BURNOUT NO CONTEXTO ORGANIZACIONAL: PROJETO EXTENSIONISTA
items.abstract: Burnout syndrome is an important occupational health issue associated with working conditions and work organization. This study aimed to report an educational intervention focused on raising awareness about burnout and promoting mental health among workers. This is a descriptive experience report carried out with employees of an occupational health and safety company. Active participation by the workers was observed, encouraging discussions on psychosocial risk factors, burnout prevention, and self-care. It is concluded that educational actions are a complementary strategy for promoting mental health and strengthening a preventive culture within organizations, in accordance with the guidelines of NR-1.

items.title: QUALIDADE DE VIDA NO TRABALHO E PROMOÇÃO DA SAÚDE MENTAL: PROJETO EXTENSIONISTA EM CONTEXTO ORGANIZACIONAL
items.abstract: Quality of Working Life (QWL) is an important dimension of mental health promotion in organizations. This study aimed to report and analyze an extension experience focused on promoting QWL in an occupational health and safety company in Praia Grande, São Paulo, Brazil. This qualitative and descriptive experience report was conducted by Psychology students through a dialogic lecture with 12 employees. Active participation and reports concerning time management, internal communication, and occupational stress were observed. The experience encouraged reflection on mental health and the integration of theory and practice, indicating the relevance of psychoeducational actions in organizational contexts.

items.title: Roles and Research Focus of AI in Mathematics Education: Insights from a Systematic Literature Review and Bibliometric Analysis
items.abstract: In this study, we adopted a holistic approach by integrating bibliometric analysis and systematic review methods to thoroughly evaluate the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics education and its research trends. The study aims to understand the current state of the field and provide strategic direction for future research by assessing general trends, intellectual contributions, and application potential in AI-focused mathematics education research from a multidimensional perspective. In the first phase, we conducted a content analysis of 363 articles published in high-quality journals indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database, focusing on dimensions such as publishers, method types, research designs, study groups, theoretical or conceptual frameworks, data collection techniques, preferred technologies, purposes of use, and roles. Subsequently, we conducted a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of scientific productivity, citation performance, collaboration networks, conceptual structures, thematic maps, and intellectual transformations. During this process, we followed the guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA). The findings indicate that AI technologies have been increasingly utilized in mathematics education, with significant growth observed since 2015. AI-focused mathematics education research has been predominantly concentrated in countries like the USA, China, and Germany, delving into areas such as personalized learning, assessment, feedback, and pedagogical innovations. Most studies have employed quantitative and mixed methods, with middle school and undergraduate students being the primary target groups. Bibliometric analyses reveal a rapid expansion in scientific productivity and collaboration networks, while thematic trends primarily focus on personalized learning and the integration of digital tools.

items.title: Seeing a Mind in the Machine: Human-Like Perceptions of AI and Attachment-Based Bonds with AI among University Students
items.abstract: Students today do not just use AI tools; many talk to them, confide in them, and sometimes describe them in almost personal terms. This study asked whether the extent to which students perceive AI as human-like (AI anthropomorphism) is linked to the emotional bond they report having with AI (Human–AI relationship). Using a cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 300 university students (158 men and 142 women) through convenient sampling. Anthropomorphism was assessed with the Scale of AI Anthropomorphism (SAIA; Xu et al., 2026) and the Human–AI relationship with the Experiences in Human–AI Relationships Scale (EHARS; Yang & Oshio, 2025). Reliability was good for both measures (α = .91 and .83). Anthropomorphism and Human–AI relationship were positively correlated (r = .38, p < .001), and anthropomorphism significantly predicted Human–AI relationship, accounting for roughly 14% of its variance. Male students scored higher than female students on both variables, with small effects (d = 0.28 and 0.34). Students who see more of a "mind" in AI therefore tend to report stronger attachment-related experiences with it. The implications for AI literacy, responsible technology use, and future research in Pakistan are discussed.

Going beyond the standard four-stage SAMR transformation model, the author analyzes key pedagogical dimensions, including learner autonomy, multi-layered cognitive AI roles, and human-AI co-agency. Practical aspects of technology implementation and adaptive learning ecosystems are highlighted.

items.title: Technology prioritisation and injury-burden reporting in construction safety research: a systematic analytical review
items.abstract: This systematic analytical review examines technology prioritisation patterns in construction safety technology (CST) research and how injury-burden evidence is reported and used in study rationales and evaluations. It distinguishes the documented use of injury-consequence evidence from the safety relevance of the hazards addressed and from demonstrated reductions in harm. A review of 148 peer-reviewed CST studies published between 2016, and April 2026 was conducted using Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect. Studies were coded across eight domains covering safety functions, risk contexts, data and intelligence characteristics, human–technology interaction, adoption maturity, system architecture, evaluation approaches, and burden considerations. Methodological quality was appraised using the Quality Assessment Tool for Studies with Diverse Designs (QATSDD), and threshold- and quality-stratified sensitivity analyses tested the robustness of the synthesis. The review introduces the Technology Prioritisation Logic Framework as an analytical construct for organising recurring study characteristics, together with an assessment of reported burden integration in problem framing and evaluation. Findings show that CST research is concentrated around prevention, detection/monitoring, computer vision, wearable sensing, machine learning, alerts, and managerial reporting, while severity, time loss, cost, and long-term worker impact remain weakly integrated. The findings support a shift toward burden-informed safety technology design, evaluation, and governance.

items.title: THE AUTOMATING THREAT : A Machine-Speed Defensive Architecture Against Sequential and Autonomous Cyberattacks. ST-T1024 + DTAL + A1–A17 A constructive proposal for detecting, constraining and stopping unauthorized automated action sequences
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing the economics and operational speed of cyberattacks. The growing ability of AI systems and autonomous agents to investigate targets, generate attack strategies, coordinate operations and execute successive actions creates a challenge for conventional security architectures. The critical issue is not necessarily a single malicious operation. It is the possibility of asequence of individually plausible actions that collectively produces an unauthorized result. This paper proposes a defensive architectural response combining ST-T1024, theDeterministic Trust and Authorization Layer (DTAL), and the A1–A17 agentic researchframework. The proposal separates intelligence from operational authority. An AI agent may investigate, reason, identify weaknesses and propose actions. However, its ability to execute actions remains subject to identity, authorization, information-graph relationships, link-specific costs, budgets and explicit thresholds. DTAL provides a mechanism for evaluating successive actions against an organization'sauthorization structure. ST-T1024 provides the proposed deterministic foundation for bounded decision processes. A1–A17 contribute complementary mechanisms for bounded agency, verification and behavioural analysis. The central defensive principle is straightforward:When an action sequence violates an established authorization boundary, furtherexecution must be stopped. The paper develops this proposition through illustrative attack scenarios, identifies theconditions required for effectiveness, and proposes a path toward independent validation. It does not claim that the architecture has already been experimentally proven to prevent all cyberattacks.

items.title: The Bidirectional Relations Between Perceived Parental Autonomy Support, Subjective Intergenerational Mobility and Academic Engagement in Chinese Adolescents
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Perceived parental autonomy support plays a central role in fostering adolescents' academic engagement, yet little research has simultaneously examined its bidirectional associations with academic engagement or the mechanisms explaining these links. To address this gap, this study used cross-lagged panel modeling (CLPM) and random-intercept cross-lagged panel modeling (RI-CLPM) to investigate reciprocal relationships among perceived parental autonomy support, subjective intergenerational mobility, and academic engagement, while testing the mediating role of subjective intergenerational mobility. METHODS: Participants were 738 Chinese adolescents (55.9% male; Mage = 14.58 years, SD = 0.59) who completed three waves of data collection at 6-month intervals. RESULTS: Results from the CLPM indicated reciprocal associations between perceived parental autonomy support and subjective intergenerational mobility. In contrast, the RI-CLPM revealed a more differentiated dynamic pattern: perceived parental autonomy support at T1 predicted subjective intergenerational mobility at T2, which subsequently predicted perceived parental autonomy support at T3. Furthermore, subjective intergenerational mobility predicted academic engagement only in the CLPM but not in the RI-CLPM. Importantly, both modeling approaches consistently demonstrated a stable reciprocal association between perceived parental autonomy support and academic engagement. CONCLUSION: These findings highlight the importance of considering temporal dynamics and individual differences when examining the relationships among perceived parental autonomy support, subjective intergenerational mobility, and adolescents' academic engagement. The results suggest that enhancing perceived parental autonomy support and strengthening adolescents' perceptions of intergenerational mobility may serve as vital pathways to sustain and promote long-term academic engagement.

items.title: The Problem with P vs NP Isn't the Mathematics
items.abstract: This essay challenges the idea that P vs NP adequately represents the broader limits of human and computational problem-solving. While recognizing its mathematical validity, it argues that real-world solvability depends on more than polynomial-time algorithms—including accumulated knowledge, evolving computational systems, artificial intelligence, collaboration, and physical constraints. Rather than claiming to solve P vs NP, the paper questions whether its prominence among the Millennium Prize Problems still reflects the deeper questions we should be asking about computation, intelligence, and the nature of solvability.

items.title: THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN AI USE AND CRITICAL THINKING IN EFL ACADEMIC WRITING
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has significantly transformed English as a Foreign Language (EFL) academic writing practices. AI-powered applications, particularly ChatGPT, provide students with opportunities to generate ideas, organize arguments, receive feedback, improve grammatical accuracy, and revise academic texts. However, the increasing use of these technologies has raised important questions concerning their relationship with students' critical thinking abilities. The present study examines the relationship between AI use and critical thinking in EFL academic writing, focusing on analytical reasoning, evaluation of information, argument development, independent decision-making, and reflective writing practices. A qualitative, literature-based research design is adopted to investigate how AI-assisted writing influences students' cognitive engagement and academic performance. Previous research suggests that structured AI-assisted instruction can support critical thinking when students actively evaluate generated information, question suggestions, and make independent decisions. At the same time, excessive dependence on AI-generated content may reduce opportunities for independent reasoning and original idea development. Recent empirical studies involving EFL university students have demonstrated positive associations between guided ChatGPT use, critical thinking, and writing proficiency. The study emphasizes that the educational value of AI depends not simply on the frequency of its use but on the quality of students' interaction with the technology. It concludes that AI should function as a supportive learning resource rather than a replacement for human reasoning. Integrating critical thinking activities into AI-assisted academic writing instruction may help EFL students develop stronger analytical, evaluative, and independent writing abilities.

items.title: Wer entscheidet, wenn Systeme vorentscheiden? Menschliche Kontrolle und Verantwortung in sicherheitskritischen Entscheidungskontexten – eine technikphilosophische Skizze
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly supports the interpretation, prioritisation and presentation of information in high-stakes organisational settings. Yet the formal presence of a human decision-maker does not establish effective human control. This working paper develops a socio-technical and normative perspective on human oversight in AI-supported situation assessment, with particular attention to governmental security analysis and critical electric power infrastructure in Austria and Germany. Drawing selectively on Heidegger, Schelsky and Latour, it examines how technical systems structure what becomes visible, actionable and contestable. Kant’s ideas of public justification and Jonas’s ethics of responsibility provide a normative orientation, while Ben Green’s critique of individual human oversight highlights the importance of institutional governance. Drawing on Vaughan and Elish, the paper argues that institutional oversight depends in part on organised capacities for contestation by professionals. Four analytical dimensions are proposed: epistemic pre-structuring, practical verifiability, the capacity to contest system outputs, and the attribution of responsibility. Existing empirical research in security operations centres and electricity control rooms demonstrates that the subject is already under investigation, and raises questions for comparative research. The paper also outlines a future qualitative study based on expert interviews. Its central proposition is that meaningful oversight must be studied as an organisational capability, not merely as an individual duty.

items.title: When takeovers require cognitive control: Effects of partial automation and cognitive load on driver-initiated responses to traffic hazards on urban roads
items.abstract: Partially automated driving (PAD) systems are becoming increasingly prevalent in consumer vehicles. While drivers are obliged to monitor the roadway and the system during PAD, they do not always comply with this requirement and may engage in non-driving-related tasks (NDRTs). Literature has emphasized the detrimental effects of visual-manual NDRTs on drivers' capability to takeover control from PAD while reporting negligible effects of non-visual NDRTs (e.g., hands-free phone calls) and cognitive load. However, most studies focused on alerted scenarios, with takeover requests lowering drivers' reliance on anticipation and cognitive control, masking the effects of cognitive load. Related work also examined PAD conditions alone, neglecting the combined effects of automation and cognitive load on drivers' responses. To address the gaps, we conducted a driving simulator study examining the influence of cognitive load, induced by a 2-back task, on driver-initiated responses to urban traffic hazards (e.g., crossing pedestrians, oncoming vehicles) during both manual driving and PAD. The timing and quality of driver-initiated responses were analysed separately for each hazard with detail. Results showed that driver-initiated responses during PAD were less anticipatory and relied more on cognitive control. This shift led to higher situational criticality and heightened susceptibility of responses to cognitive load during PAD. Hazard characteristics such as motion speed and cue ambiguity appeared to influence cognitive load effects and warrant systematic examination in future work. Together, these findings underscore an elevated safety risk associated with cognitive load during PAD, especially in scenarios requiring cognitively demanding, driver-initiated intervention.

items.title: Who Authorizes Human–AI Decision Cooperation?
items.abstract: Human oversight in AI-assisted decision-making is often examined from the moment a person receives a recommendation. Yet the information, alternatives and conditions available to that person may already have been shaped by earlier technical and institutional choices. Drawing on established research in organisational decision theory, agenda-setting power, system-level bureaucracy, technological due process and sociotechnical accountability, this working paper examines a question at their intersection: who governs the conditions under which a human–AI decision becomes possible, and who can legitimately examine or reconsider those conditions? The paper explores the relationship between authority over institutional decisions and authority over their formation, considering how responsibilities and effective oversight capabilities may be distributed across organisations and affected by subsequent changes. It situates this discussion within existing European AI governance and data-protection law. Its proposed contribution is integrative rather than a claim of originality for the individual concepts involved. The paper does not presume that additional external authorisation is necessary, nor does it claim empirical validation of the proposed analytical perspective. Published within ID∆AC Research as a public discussion working paper, this contribution invites critical engagement from researchers and practitioners in law, organisational theory, AI governance, sociotechnical systems and institutional accountability. Comments, counterarguments, overlooked intellectual precedents and alternative institutional interpretations are particularly welcome. The purpose is to refine the question through informed disagreement and interdisciplinary exchange. Research correspondence: contact@iddac.eu Research affiliation: ID∆AC Research, ID∆AC – Independent Decision & Accountability Consulting. Status: Public discussion working paper. Not peer reviewed. Empirical validation remains open.

items.title: ภาวะผู้นำกับการสร้าง Employee Engagement
items.abstract: This academic article aims to examine and analyze the systematic relationship between leadership and the creation of Employee Engagement, which is considered a strategic variable directly affecting organizational performance and sustainability within the context of today’s socio-economic environment. Through content analysis of instructional documents and contemporary research studies, the literature review reveals that Employee Engagement is a significant variable reflecting employees’ psychological characteristics, including commitment, dedication, and willingness to perform at their full potential. These characteristics demonstrate a statistically significant positive relationship with organizational performance. Furthermore, the study found that leadership, particularly Transformational Leadership and Servant Leadership, plays a causal role in enhancing engagement levels through several mechanisms, including the creation of intrinsic motivation, emotional and psychological support, effective organizational communication, and the cultivation of meaningfulness in work. In addition, contextual factors such as organizational culture and human resource management policies serve as supporting variables that strengthen and sustain engagement levels over time. Organizations that maintain a positive working environment are more capable of managing engagement effectively. This article also proposes the Leadership–Engagement Integration Model as a new body of knowledge that can be applied in digital-era organizations. The model emphasizes the development of leaders through Agile Leadership alongside the application of technology and data analytics to measure and analyze engagement levels concretely. In conclusion, leadership is regarded as a strategic factor with significant implications for the development of Employee Engagement and serves as a fundamental foundation for long-term organizational success.

items.title: A New Era for Mathematics: The Future with Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This paper addresses the ongoing debate on whether AI helps accelerate developments in the field of Mathematics or does it come at a greater cost. It explores the very principles and foundations that have guided mathematicians for centuries in the context of today’s issue. It then examines the tension between accelerating mathematical discovery through automated proof generation and preserving human intuition, verification, and intellectual rigor. The paper does not seek to dismiss the organizations involved in building the artificial intelligence tools, rather it aims to advocate for a balanced approach where these technologies can be sustainably integrated into mathematical working, rather than completely replacing human intuition and rigour.

items.abstract: Objective: To understand the perception and level of knowledge of nursing students regarding the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in healthcare services. Methods: This was an exploratory-descriptive, cross-sectional and quantitative study, conducted with 302 students from two educational institutions in Altamira, Pará. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire addressing perceived usefulness, ease of use from the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and ethical dilemmas. The analysis occurred via descriptive statistics using Microsoft Excel® software. The study was approved by a Research Ethics Committee. Results: The sample presented a female majority (75.8%) and brown skin color (60.6%). The "Invisibility Paradox" phenomenon was found: although 81.5% affirmed prior contact with AI, 46.4% failed to recognize its clinical applications, and 56.6% judged their knowledge as basic. Through the TAM model, utility (time optimization and diagnostic support) is recognized, but the need for extensive training acts as a barrier. Ethically, decision opacity and the replacement of clinical judgment (totally feared by 40.7%) are the greatest challenges. Conclusion: It is concluded that AI integration is accepted by students as clinical support, provided it preserves the autonomy of the augmented nurse and humanized care.

items.title: A Study on the Role of Artificial Intelligence in Enhancing Academic Performance
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an important technological advancement in the field of education. It supports students through personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessments, and virtual academic assistance. The use of Artificial Intelligence helps students improve their learning efficiency, understanding of subjects, and overall academic performance. This study aims to analyse the role of Artificial Intelligence in enhancing academic performance among students. The study focuses on students’ awareness, usage, and perception of AI-based educational tools. Primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire, and secondary data were collected from journals, books, and research articles. The study reveals that Artificial Intelligence has a positive influence on students’ academic performance, though challenges such as lack of awareness and technical skills still exist. Suitable suggestions are provided to improve the effective use of Artificial Intelligence in the academic environment.

items.title: AI IN HIGHER EDUCATION: GLOBAL TRENDS AND STRATEGIES FOR INSTITUTIONAL SUCCESS IN THE ARAB REGION
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education worldwide, reshaping teaching, learning, assessment, student support, and institutional governance. Recent systematic reviews show a rapid growth of AI applications in higher education but highlight persistent gaps in ethics, evidence, and policy coherence. In the Arab region, AI adoption is unfolding within ambitious national digital transformation agendas, including UAE’s National Strategy for AI 2031, Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, and Oman Vision 2040, which explicitly position AI as a strategic lever for human capital development and economic diversification. Arab universities are experimenting with generative AI in teaching and student support, deploying chatbots, analytics, and AI-enabled curricula, while grappling with issues of academic integrity, equity, and institutional readiness. This article synthesizes global and regional evidence on AI in higher education, with particular attention to generative AI and its implications for the Arab region. It proposes the Strategic AI in Higher Education (SAIHE) framework, designed as a practical guide for institutional leaders. The framework integrates five domains Vision and Strategy; Governance, Ethics and Risk; Teaching, Learning and Assessment; Student Success and Experience; and Capacity, Culture and Infrastructure underpinned by a cross-cutting layer of evidence and continuous improvement. The article concludes by outlining implications for institutional leaders, quality assurance bodies, and policymakers, and identifies directions for future research on AI-enabled transformation in Arab higher education systems.

items.title: AI-DRIVEN STRATEGIC LEADERSHIP, AI ADOPTION AND PERCEIVED ORGANISATIONAL ADAPTABILITY IN ACCRA, GHANA
items.abstract: This study examined the individual and joint associations of AI-driven strategic leadership and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption with perceived organisational adaptability among private organisations in Accra, Ghana. A quantitative-priority mixed-methods, descriptive-correlational design combined questionnaires from 799 respondents (399 leaders and 400 employees) in 84 organisations with 25 key-informant interviews. Random-intercept multilevel regression assessed leadership and adoption while adjusting for respondent category, organisation size, tenure and sector; supplementary models and thematic analysis examined robustness and context. Organisation-level clustering was meaningful (intraclass correlations = .240-.414). Adding AI-driven strategic leadership to the controls model was associated with greater perceived adaptability (B = 0.577, 95% CI [0.511, 0.643], p< .001), increasing marginal R² from .210 to .428. In the joint model, leadership remained the larger correlate (B = 0.494, p< .001), while adoption contributed a smaller independent association (B = 0.153, p< .001); marginal R² reached .448. Respondent-category interactions were not significant. None of seven exploratory leadership dimensions remained individually significant after Holm adjustment. Findings support the relevance of integrated leadership practices beyond reported AI access, but the cross-sectional self-report design does not establish causality. Organisations should combine documented AI direction, workforce preparation, governance and objective monitoring of adaptation.

items.title: AI-generated support, worked examples, and script-based learning in undergraduate physics: A comparative study
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to support students during learning and problem solving, but its instructional value depends on how it is embedded in established learning approaches. Worked examples guide learners through the steps and reasoning of a solution; conversational AI may extend them by responding to individual questions. To isolate this added value, we compared a chatbot-delivered intelligent worked example with a matched static worked example and a lecture script. Nine recitation groups in an undergraduate electrodynamics course were cluster-randomized to the three conditions, and 86 students worked individually on a Gauss's law problem. Concept-test accuracy and self-efficacy increased significantly in all conditions, but changes did not differ significantly between groups (p=.07 for concept-test accuracy and p=.38 for self-efficacy). Four weeks later, in a reduced sample with selective participation and pre-existing group differences, students in the static worked-example condition scored higher than those in the script condition (p=.004, d=1.22), whereas the two worked-example conditions did not differ significantly. Usability, but not perceived educational value, was higher for the intelligent worked example than for the script (p=.011, d=0.88). In a subsequent homework assignment on Ampere's law with free choice of learning material (N=46), 62-71% of students in each condition reported using only the static worked example, at most 8% used exclusively the intelligent one, and 15-31% used neither. Thus, conversational delivery showed no clear additional learning benefit under the present conditions. More broadly, a learning format that is rated favorably need not be the one students voluntarily adopt.

items.title: Appropriating managerial identity regulation through collective tactics: The case of environmental insider activism
items.abstract: How can employee groups influence identity regulation within their organisation? While recognising that employees have agency in their response to organisational identity control, the literature has largely positioned identity regulation as a managerial prerogative enforced through disciplinary power. Some research, however, finds that groups of employees are able to shape their members’ identities and oppose or negotiate managerial attempts to influence them. This article extends the identity regulation research by showing how employee groups can go beyond merely reacting to managerial identity regulation; they can also appropriate and redirect it to influence other employees. Using an in-depth case study, we analyse how an environmental insider activist group managed to do so through two interrelated tactics: augmenting the ideal employee identity built and promoted by management and repurposing existing identity regulation practices and discourses. By demonstrating how employee groups without disciplinary power can appropriate and transform managerial identity regulation for a cause they care about, these findings contribute to knowledge on identity regulation dynamics within organisations and on the relationships between identity regulation and broader societal norms.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is considered as a field of computer science dedicated to creating an integrated machine capable of performing tasks that systematically requires human intelligence such as learning, reasoning, decision or problem-solving. Curriculum development at the basic education is a foundational standard for greater advancement in Multicultural paradigm. The current focus has shifted from "using tech" to "integrating intelligence" that supports both the teacher and the learner. Recommendations: Integrating AI into classroom assessment offers the potential to enhance efficiency, objectivity, and pedagogical decision-making. The following assertions are made to have a robust foundational AI education in the country: Pilot Testing & Capacity Building Professional Development (TPD): Implement continuous, hands-on training for primary school teachers focusing on facilitation techniques, cross-curricular planning, and formative assessment. Conclusion: AI usage has emerged as an integral part of several sectors, altering the way businesses and personnel engage with technology. The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence within educational contexts presents significant opportunities for refining classroom assessment methodologies through the deployment o AI-driven instruments (Ayo, 2025).

items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Literacy as a Predictor of Teachers' Pedagogical Innovation and Technology Integration
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing teachers’ instructional planning, learning design, assessment, feedback, and professional work. This study examined whether teachers’ AI literacy predicts pedagogical innovation and technology integration among the 68 permanent teachers of Maydolong National High School, Maydolong District, Eastern Samar. A quantitative, non-experimental predictive-correlational design was used, with total population sampling. Data were gathered through an adapted questionnaire measuring AI literacy, pedagogical innovation, technology integration, technology access, AI experience, and AI-related training. The findings showed very high AI literacy (M = 4.587, SD = 0.409), very high pedagogical innovation (M = 4.423, SD = 0.490), and very high frequency of technology integration (M = 4.366, SD = 0.462). Critical Evaluation of AI was the highest AI-literacy dimension (M = 4.728), while AI for Professional Learning was the lowest, although still very high (M = 4.403). Pearson correlation revealed a strong positive relationship between AI literacy and pedagogical innovation (r = .685, p < .001), but a negligible and non-significant relationship between AI literacy and general technology integration (r = -.009, p = .940). Simple linear regression showed that AI literacy significantly predicted pedagogical innovation, explaining 47.0% of its variance (β = .685, R² = .470, p < .001), but did not predict technology integration (β = -.009, R² ≈ .000, p = .940). The findings indicate that AI literacy is particularly relevant to pedagogical innovation, whereas broader technology integration is likely shaped by additional contextual factors such as infrastructure, access, professional development, and institutional support.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and digitalization reinforce inequality in developing countries
items.abstract: Digitalization and artificial intelligence (AI) can expand access, productivity, and service delivery in developing countries, yet their benefits are distributed unevenly and may reinforce pre-existing structural inequalities. This systematic review distinguishes foundational digitalization from more computationally intensive AI applications and re-audits the evidence base in response to concerns about scope and reproducibility. Of the 75 publications retained in the broader literature corpus, 57 meet the prespecified criteria for the systematic synthesis; 18 are retained only as contextual/background literature and are not included in evidence counts. The review uses PRISMA 2020 reporting principles and a design-specific Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) procedure for eligible empirical studies. The thematic synthesis presents four interconnected mechanisms: unequal digital and AI capabilities, workforce and value-distribution pressures, uneven socio-economic results, and governance constraints. These are integrated into the ‘Vicious Cycle of Techno-Dependency’ as an interpretive framework, not a tested causal model. Evidence indicates that the strength and form of these mechanisms vary across country contexts and institutional capacities. Recent post-search studies from Brazil, India, and Indonesia further suggest that data-protection and sovereignty initiatives can strengthen accountability, but their effectiveness is conditional and remains incomplete. Policy priorities therefore include locally appropriate infrastructure and skills investment, participatory data governance, algorithmic accountability, and evaluation of implementation outcomes rather than reliance on formal policy adoption alone.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Driver of Managerial Competency Transformation: An Empirical Study of Telecommunications Operators in Tunisia
items.abstract: Résumé Objectif : Cet article examine comment l’intelligence artificielle (IA) transforme les compétences managériales dans le secteur tunisien des télécommunications, industrie fortement numérisée où les algorithmes soutiennent la segmentation de la clientèle, la maintenance prédictive et l’optimisation des réseaux. Les mécanismes par lesquels l’IA remodèle les compétences des managers demeurent peu explorés, en particulier dans les économies émergentes d’Afrique du Nord. Approche méthodologique : L’étude adopte une démarche quantitative, positiviste et hypothético-déductive. Mobilisant les théories des capacités dynamiques et des systèmes sociotechniques, complétées par les modèles d’acceptation technologique et la perspective institutionnelle, elle teste un modèle reliant l’IA, la confiance dans l’IA et la culture organisationnelle (variable modératrice) à quatre familles de compétences : collaboratives, augmentées, centrées sur l’humain et émergentes. L’IA est modélisée comme un construit réflexif de second ordre à six dimensions. Les données, recueillies par questionnaire auto-administré (échelles de Likert à sept points), sont analysées par PLS-SEM (SmartPLS 4.0, 5 000 rééchantillonnages). Les hypothèses testent les effets directs des six dimensions de l’IA et les effets d’interaction de quatre dimensions culturelles (adoption, soutien organisationnel, intégration stratégique et formation). Échantillon questionné : 72 cadres supérieurs et top managers de Tunisie Télécom, Ooredoo et Orange (24 par opérateur), interrogés sur une période de quatre mois. Résultats : L’IA exerce un effet positif et significatif sur les compétences collaboratives (β = 0,53 ; p < 0,001) et augmentées (β = 0,41 ; p < 0,001). L’interaction homme-IA est le prédicteur le plus fort des compétences collaboratives (β = 0,71), et la confiance dans l’IA (β = 0,38) agit comme un mécanisme actif de développement des compétences. Les coefficients d’interaction, négatifs, suggèrent que la culture organisationnelle standardise l’influence de l’IA plutôt qu’elle ne l’amplifie. Originalité et implications : L’étude propose un modèle intégrateur IA–compétences–culture et une grille à quatre familles de compétences, et en tire des implications pour le recrutement, la formation continue, la construction de la confiance et la gouvernance de l’IA. Limites : Taille de l’échantillon et caractère transversal. Mots clés : intelligence artificielle ; compétences managériales ; transformation numérique ; PLS-SEM ; économies émergentes ; télécommunications ; Tunisie Abstract Purpose: This article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) transforms managerial competencies in the Tunisian telecommunications sector, a highly digitalized industry in which algorithms support customer segmentation, predictive maintenance and network optimization. The mechanisms through which AI reshapes managers’ skills remain under-explored, particularly in North African emerging economies. Design/methodology/approach: The study adopts a quantitative, positivist and hypothetico-deductive approach. Drawing on dynamic capabilities and sociotechnical systems theories, complemented by technology acceptance models and an institutional perspective, it tests a model linking AI, trust in AI and organizational culture (moderator) to four families of competencies: collaborative, augmented, human-centric and emerging. AI is modeled as a second-order reflective construct with six dimensions. Data were collected through a self-administered questionnaire (seven-point Likert scales) and analyzed with PLS-SEM (SmartPLS 4.0, 5,000 bootstrap resamples). The hypotheses test the direct effects of the six AI dimensions and the interaction effects of four cultural dimensions (adoption, organizational support, strategic integration and training). Sample: 72 senior managers and top executives of Tunisie Télécom, Ooredoo and Orange (24 per operator), surveyed over four months. Findings: AI has a positive and significant effect on collaborative (β = 0.53; p < 0.001) and augmented competencies (β = 0.41; p < 0.001). Human–AI interaction is the strongest predictor of collaborative competencies (β = 0.71), and trust in AI (β = 0.38) acts as an active mechanism of competency development. The negative interaction coefficients suggest that organizational culture standardizes the influence of AI rather than amplifying it. Originality and implications: The study proposes an integrative AI–competencies–culture model and a four-family competency framework, and derives implications for recruitment, continuous training, trust building and AI governance. items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Dental Traumatology: A Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic, Predictive, and Decision-Support Performance
items.abstract: Introduction and aims Although artificial intelligence (AI) may improve early Traumatic dental injury (TDI) management, evidence across imaging diagnosis, risk prediction, large language model (LLM)-based decision support, and patient education remains unsynthesised. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, with PRISMA-AI principles consulted, we searched eight databases through 14 March 2026 for original studies evaluating AI in dental trauma. Methodological quality was appraised with design-specific tools (QUADAS-2, QUADAS-AI, PROBAST+AI, JBI Critical Appraisal Checklists, and RoB 2), supplemented by a structured AI-specific framework for LLM and chatbot evaluations. Reconstructable binary correctness data from non-clinical LLM, chatbot, or AI-assisted workflow studies were pooled using a random-effects meta-analysis of logit-transformed proportions with exploratory subgroup, sensitivity, and leave-one-out analyses, while remaining studies were synthesised descriptively. Results Thirty-seven studies spanning six evidence domains were included. Across 11 non-clinical LLM/chatbot evaluations, pooled accuracy was 0.798 (95% CI: 0.665-0.887), with extreme heterogeneity (I² = 99.66%) and a wide 95% PI (0.415-0.956), reflecting variability in systems, prompting strategies, and evaluation methods rather than a clinical performance benchmark. Disease-specific or workflow-enhanced systems (3 studies) showed numerically higher accuracy than general-purpose LLMs (8 studies; 0.957 versus 0.755), but the difference was not statistically supported (meta-regression P = .150), nor were other moderators. Imaging deep learning models (4 studies), predictive pipelines (4 studies), and one prospective clinical-validation study reported high task-specific performance (accuracy up to 0.919, mean average precision up to 0.995, and diagnostic accuracy up to 0.949). Overall, 11 studies were at high risk of bias and 25 at moderate risk. Conclusion Guideline-grounded tools show promise for time-critical TDIs; however, predominantly non-clinical, highly heterogeneous and moderate-to-high-risk evidence does not support readiness for clinical triage. Prospective, version-locked, independently and externally validated real-world clinical studies with transparent AI-specific reporting are needed before AI systems are recommended for clinical triage or emergency dental decision-making. Clinical relevance AI showed promising but highly variable accuracy in dental trauma (pooled 0.798 across 11 non-clinical studies; 95% PI: 0.415-0.956). Guideline-anchored and disease-specific systems performed numerically better than general-purpose LLMs, although this indirect difference was not statistically confirmed. These tools may support non-specialists in time-critical TDIs but require independent external validation and prospective real-world assessment before being recommended for clinical triage.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Challenges and Managerial Risks
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become a near-universal part of students’ academic practice, confronting universities with challenges that reach beyond technology to the core of teaching and assessment. This article is an integrative narrative review of peer-reviewed studies, preprints and policy documents published mainly between 2023 and 2026. It examines the crisis in the validity of knowledge assessment and the unreliability of AI detectors; cognitive dependence, metacognitive laziness and the erosion of critical thinking; digital inequality; the meta-analytic evidence on learning effects; and the regulatory framework set by UNESCO, the OECD and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. The cross-cutting theme is the “performance–learning gap”: GenAI reliably improves task performance, but genuine learning gains depend on teacher support, pedagogical guardrails and the way students use the tool, and they often disappear when knowledge is assessed without AI. Particular attention is given to Georgia, where AI uptake is already high while the institutional response remains fragmented. The article proposes structural reform of assessment, a five-stage institutional pilot model for Georgian universities, a practical formula for students (“think first, ask AI, then evaluate critically”) and a research agenda of six priority directions.

items.title: Artificial intelligence large language models and the threat to human health – A consensus statement by AAIO
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by patients, clinicians, and health organizations to obtain, summarize, and generate medical information. Although these tools can improve access to information and reduce communication barriers, their fluent output can obscure important limitations. This narrative review examines how LLMs may harm human health through interacting technical, cognitive, clinical, and societal mechanisms. Risks include fabricated or incomplete information, contextually inappropriate advice, failure to identify emergencies, unsafe medication or procedural guidance, sycophantic responses to leading questions, and excessive user reliance. Vulnerable people seeking mental health support may be particularly susceptible to validating or dependency-promoting interactions. Beyond individual encounters, LLMs can amplify health misinformation, contaminate evidence-retrieval systems, reproduce inequities, expose sensitive health data, and undermine scientific integrity. Case reports and recent litigation illustrate potential severity but do not establish the incidence of harm or prove causation. Risk reduction requires complementary action by patients, clinicians, developers, health systems, and regulators. LLMs should be treated as fallible communication tools rather than autonomous clinicians: High-stakes outputs require independent verification, identifiable data require appropriate protection, and urgent symptoms require conventional emergency assessment. Evaluation using realistic patient conversations, sustained human oversight, and transparent post-deployment monitoring is essential if the benefits of medical LLMs are to be realized without avoidable harm. Real-world cases have been included to provide greater clarity on the gravity of the situation and the finer points of jurisprudence under consideration.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Learning and Mathematical Problem-Solving Skills among Senior High School Students
items.abstract: This study examined the relationship between artificial intelligence-assisted learning and mathematical problem-solving skills among Grade 12 students at Sulu National High School, Sulu, Philippines. Anchored in instructional scaffolding and self-regulated learning principles, the study employed a quantitative, cross-sectional, descriptive-correlational research design using a structured questionnaire and mathematical problem-solving assessment. An illustrative dataset comprising 350 student records was analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, analysis of variance, and multiple linear regression. The analysis yielded an overall mean of 3.37 for AI-assisted learning and an average mathematical performance score of 70.04%. Problem comprehension obtained the highest performance score (76.96%), while verification and interpretation recorded the lowest (63.18%). A statistically significant moderate positive relationship was identified between AI-assisted learning and mathematical problem-solving performance (r = 0.386, p < .001). Regression analysis indicated that AI-assisted learning dimensions explained 15.72% of the variance in mathematical performance, with accessibility and utilization emerging as a significant predictor. The findings suggested that AI-assisted learning could support mathematical understanding and problem-solving, although independent verification and critical evaluation remained important areas for improvement. The study recommended integrating AI-supported instruction with independent mathematical assessments, teacher guidance, and responsible technology utilization. Its educational implications aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) and Sustainable Development Goal 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure) by promoting inclusive learning opportunities and responsible educational innovation. The proposed approach could contribute to educational and institutional sustainability by informing mathematics instruction, digital learning policies, and the development of independent problem-solving competencies. Further empirical validation was necessary to establish the applicability of these findings to the target student population.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Supported Professional Development and Digital Teaching Competence Among University Lecturers: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education is transforming teaching and learning practices and creating new opportunities for the professional development of university lecturers. AI-supported professional development has the potential to strengthen lecturers' digital teaching competence through personalized learning, intelligent feedback, adaptive instruction, and AI-assisted pedagogical practices. However, the nature, effectiveness, and implications of these interventions remain insufficiently synthesized. This systematic review examines the relationship between AI-supported professional development and digital teaching competence among university lecturers. The review adopts a systematic literature review approach guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. Relevant empirical studies were identified through a structured literature search and assessed against predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria through searches of selected academic databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC and Google Scholar. AI-supported professional development was operationally defined as professional learning activities incorporating identifiable artificial intelligence capabilities, including generative AI applications, intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning technologies, conversational AI, and AI-powered feedback systems. Conventional digital technologies without identifiable AI functionality were distinguished from AI-supported interventions. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, with two reviewers independently conducting the assessments and resolving disagreements through discussion and consensus. The review synthesizes evidence on the ways AI-supported professional development can contribute to university lecturers' digital teaching competence, particularly in digital pedagogical knowledge, technology integration, instructional design, assessment practices, personalized learning, and reflective teaching. In conclusion, AI-supported professional development represents a potentially valuable approach to strengthening university lecturers' digital teaching competence. The review highlights the need for context-sensitive professional development frameworks that integrate AI competencies with broader digital pedagogical capabilities.

items.title: Authority bias in Human-AI decision making: The effects of AI appraisals and journal cues in abstract screening
items.abstract: Human-AI collaboration is increasingly embedded in decision-making tasks, including systematic reviewing workflows such as title and abstract screening. Yet humans as final arbiters remain susceptible to peripheral cues, leaving these hybrid workflows vulnerable to systematic bias. This paper examined how two authority cues, namely AI appraisals and journal prestige, influence screening judgments. Across three preregistered experiments, we employed an identical 3 × 3 mixed design in which participants were randomly assigned to receive AI recommendations, AI disapprovals, or no AI appraisal, while evaluating abstracts presented with prestigious journal labels, non-prestigious journal labels, or no journal information. Across Western graduate students, Asian bachelor’s-degree holders, and Western professionals (total N = 977), AI appraisals produced robust and symmetric shifts in screening decisions: recommendations increased erroneous inclusion of irrelevant abstracts, whereas disapprovals increased erroneous exclusion of relevant abstracts. Journal information produced weaker and more asymmetric effects. Prestigious labels increased erroneous inclusion of irrelevant abstracts, whereas non-prestigious labels did not increase erroneous exclusion of relevant abstracts. Comparisons with the no-journal-information condition further suggested that the availability of journal information may itself influence inclusion decisions. These findings show that AI appraisals and journal information can both bias abstract screening, but through distinct patterns of influence, highlighting the need to design AI-aided screening systems that support independent evaluation of task-relevant information.

items.title: Axiological Problems of Artificial Intelligence in Education: Between Technological Efficiency and the Humanization of Learning
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education offers opportunities to improve efficiency, personalize learning, and support educational activities. However, these benefits raise an axiological question concerning the extent to which technological efficiency contributes to meaningful learning and human development. This article examines the axiological problems associated with the use of AI in education, particularly the tension between technological efficiency and the humanization of learning. Using a literature review approach, this study synthesizes scholarly literature to examine educational values, pedagogical implications, and ethical considerations in AI integration. Through thematic comparison, the synthesis identifies recurring issues and conceptual relationships among the instrumental benefits of AI, student agency, pedagogical relationships, and ethical responsibilities in its use. These relationships are integrated into a conceptual framework comprising four interconnected dimensions: instrumental value, student agency, pedagogical relationships, and ethical-contextual responsibility. The framework emphasizes that the educational value of AI cannot be determined solely by efficiency or the automation of learning activities, but should be assessed in terms of students’ independent thinking, the quality of pedagogical interactions, and ethical principles and contextual needs. This study offers an axiological perspective that connects these four dimensions to evaluate AI adoption in education, positioning technological efficiency as one consideration rather than the sole criterion of educational value. Since the proposed framework is developed through a conceptual synthesis of literature, further research is needed to examine its applicability across different educational contexts.

items.title: Beyond Availability: Understanding Employee Underutilization of Employer-Sponsored Employee Assistance Programs for Mental Health Care - An Integrative Theoretical Review and Recommendations
items.abstract: Employee Assistance Programs (EAPs) have become one of the most widely implemented organizational interventions designed to promote employee mental health and well-being. Over the past five decades, EAPs have evolved from occupational alcoholism programs into comprehensive behavioral health resources. Despite extensive employer investment and substantial evidence demonstrating favorable clinical and organizational outcomes, employee utilization rates remain consistently low relative to the prevalence of psychological distress within the workforce. This discrepancy presents an important theoretical and practical question: Why do employees frequently decline employer-sponsored mental health services that are confidential, readily accessible, and provided at little or no personal cost? This integrative review synthesizes research from organizational behavior, occupational health psychology, counseling psychology, human resource management, and health psychology to develop a comprehensive explanation for employee underutilization of EAP services. Rather than attributing low utilization to a lack of awareness or accessibility alone, the review argues that employees engage in a multidimensional decision-making process in which perceived organizational, interpersonal, and professional risks frequently outweigh anticipated psychological benefits. The review integrates evidence from six complementary theoretical perspectives—the Health Belief Model, Theory of Planned Behavior, Self-Stigma Theory, Organizational Trust Theory, Psychological Safety Theory, and Social Exchange Theory—to explain how individual beliefs and organizational conditions jointly influence help-seeking behavior. The paper concludes by proposing an integrated conceptual framework in which leadership behavior, organizational culture, confidentiality perceptions, workplace norms, and employee trust interact with individual cognitive appraisals to determine EAP utilization. Implications for organizational leaders, human resource professionals, and future research are discussed.

items.title: Beyond physical relief: technology-based respite and the cognitive offloading of family caregivers—a scoping review
items.abstract: Background and Objectives Technology-based respite may address systemic barriers in caregiver support, yet evidence remains fragmented. This scoping review maps and synthesizes the characteristics, mechanisms, and outcomes of technology-based interventions providing respite for family caregivers of older adults. Research Design and Methods Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, nine databases were searched (2000–2025) for empirical studies evaluating technology-based respite. Guided by the sociotechnical model, descriptive content analysis developed a functional taxonomy and charted outcomes and implementation barriers. Results Twenty-five reports (22 independent studies) formed a five-category taxonomy: (1) Environmental Monitoring and Alert Systems (n = 11); (2) Care Recipient–Directed Technologies (n = 4); (3) Technology-Mediated Substitute Care (n = 4); (4) Caregiver–Directed Support (n = 2); and (5) Personalized Coaching (n = 1). At the study level, most interventions (82%, 18 of 22 independent studies) provided psychological respite (cognitive offloading) rather than physical substitution. Primary outcomes were enhanced peace of mind and reduced anxiety. Barriers were largely socio-institutional (e.g., professional gatekeeping) rather than purely technological. Discussion and Implications Technology-based respite functions through cognitive reassurance, redefining traditional respite. A “facilitator paradox” emerged: technologies may increase care burden if not passive or professionally supported; this hypothesis warrants direct testing. Future research should explore how to better achieve sociotechnical alignment, including prioritizing passive systems and addressing institutional referral bottlenecks.

items.title: Beyond Placement Duration: Workplace Affordances, Constraints and Student Agency in a Work-Based Learning Programme
items.abstract: A twelve-month industry placement gives undergraduates time to encounter authentic work, but duration alone cannot ensure meaningful learning. This study examines the workplace conditions that support or constrain learning among students in a Malaysian liberal education degree with multidisciplinary study pathways and a structured twelve-month work-based learning (WBL) component. Thirteen students from one programme described specific workplace episodes in individual interviews informed by behavioural event interviewing; accounts were examined through reflexive thematic analysis. Five themes were developed: (1) access to meaningful work is distributed rather than guaranteed; (2) everyday problems become learning opportunities through repair and guidance; (3) learning is mediated by relationships and organisational rules; (4) organisational pressures can reduce opportunities to learn; and (5) students negotiate ways to learn within workplace constraints. Students reported that trusted assignments created opportunities to practise judgement and understand the consequences of their actions. Supportive feedback helped them learn from errors, whereas exclusion from information, changing supervisors and heavy workloads restricted participation. Hierarchy and limited voice also emerged in their accounts, although workplace culture were not measured. These single-programme, student-reported experiences were not corroborated by supervisors and do not support sector-wide generalisation. This exploratory study proposes development of mid-placement task and feedback audit for joint academic-industry review. Overall, quality in long-duration WBL depends on meaningful task access, responsive guidance and appropriate discretion, rather than time spent in industry alone.

items.title: Beyond Technological Acceptance: Understanding the Influence of AI-Induced Job Insecurity, Career Adaptability, and Organisational Support on Employee Readiness for AI-Driven HR Transformation
items.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into human resource management is transforming recruitment, employee development, performance evaluation, workforce planning and employee engagement. Although technological acceptance has received considerable research attention, employee readiness for AI-driven HR transformation cannot be explained solely through perceived usefulness, ease of use or intention to use technology. Employees may simultaneously recognise the potential benefits of AI and experience concerns regarding job displacement, skill obsolescence, professional identity and future career opportunities. This study develops and examines an integrated framework explaining employee readiness for AI-driven HR transformation through three interrelated dimensions: AI-induced job insecurity, career adaptability and perceived organisational support. Drawing on Conservation of Resources Theory, Career Construction Theory and the Job Demands–Resources perspective, the study proposes that AI-induced job insecurity negatively influences employee readiness, whereas career adaptability and perceived organisational support positively influence readiness. It further proposes that career adaptability and perceived organisational support moderate the negative relationship between AI-induced job insecurity and employee readiness. For demonstrating the proposed analytical approach, an illustrative quantitative dataset of 400 Indian IT employees is constructed. The hypothetical analysis indicates a negative association between AI-induced job insecurity and employee readiness, while career adaptability and perceived organisational support demonstrate positive associations. The illustrative moderation results also suggest that career adaptability and organisational support may reduce the adverse relationship between AI-induced job insecurity and readiness. These numerical findings are simulated and should not be interpreted as actual field evidence. The paper contributes a resource-oriented explanation of employee readiness that moves beyond conventional technology acceptance and offers a framework for future empirical investigation in India's technology-intensive employment environment.

items.title: Beyond Traditional Teaching: Exploring Teachers’ Perceptions and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education
items.abstract: This study investigated teachers’ beliefs, attitudes, awareness, and perceived challenges regarding the utilization of artificial intelligence (AI) in teaching and learning at higher education institutions in Multan District, Pakistan. A descriptive quantitative survey design was employed. Data were collected through an online, self-structured questionnaire comprising 45 statements organized into three domains: awareness of AI tools, perceived impact on teaching effectiveness, student engagement and assessment, and challenges associated with AI use. Although the thesis reports that 290 faculty members were selected, 163 completed questionnaires (67 male and 96 female) were included in the reported analysis. Frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations were used for descriptive analysis, while independent-samples t-tests and one-way ANOVA were used to examine group differences. Overall, respondents expressed favorable perceptions of AI and its potential contribution to routine academic tasks, lesson preparation, personalized learning, instructional methods, assessment design, and feedback. Lack of training, insufficient technological infrastructure, limited institutional support, ethical concerns, data privacy, and academic dishonesty were identified as important barriers. Department-based differences were statistically significant across all three perception domains. Gender differences were significant for awareness and perceived impact but not for challenges; no significant differences were reported by teaching sector, teaching experience, academic qualification, or academic position. The study concludes that meaningful AI integration requires teacher development, institutional support, adequate infrastructure, and clear ethical and academic policies. As the data represent teachers’ perceptions, the findings should not be interpreted as direct evidence of improved student achievement.

items.title: Bloom’s Taxonomy in the Age of Generative AI: From Creation To Responsible Judgement Through Verify, Orchestrate, and Reflect (VOR)
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education is challenging established assumptions about the relationship between student-produced artefacts and evidence of cognitive achievement. This perspective paper argues that these developments do not render Bloom's Taxonomy dated, but require its reinterpretation for learning environments in which cognitive work can be distributed between learners and AI systems. The perspective retains Bloom's six cognitive processes of Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, and Create while reconsidering how each is demonstrated when AI can retrieve information, generate content, analyse problems, and contribute to creative production. AI literacy is positioned as an enabling capability that operates across all levels rather than as an additional cognitive category. The paper further proposes Verify, Orchestrate, and Reflect (VOR) as three cross-cutting capabilities for AI-mediated learning. Verify concerns epistemic judgement and the ability to establish the credibility and evidential basis of information; Orchestrate concerns the strategic allocation, coordination, and supervision of cognitive work across human and AI resources; and Reflect concerns the ability to examine, explain, and take ownership of the reasoning and decisions underpinning an outcome. Their integration supports responsible judgement, conceptualised not as a seventh level of Bloom's hierarchy but as an emergent quality of higher-order performance. The paper therefore proposes a shift from production-centred evidence of learning to judgement-centred evidence, arguing that creation remains important but its educational value increasingly depends on the quality of human judgement surrounding it. The paper develops implications for assessment through oral defence, authentic tasks, process documentation, AI critique, and verification-focused activities. The proposed framework provides a basis for curriculum and assessment design that preserves Bloom's enduring emphasis on cognitive complexity while responding to the epistemic, strategic, and reflective demands of human-AI learning environments.
