items.title: Bounded AI Assistance in Higher Education: Re-Aligning Pedagogy, Assessment and Institutional Governance
items.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has led universities and other higher education institutions to rethink the ways in which knowledge is conveyed, learning is facilitated, and academic performance is evaluated. While such technologies present possibilities for tailored explanations, feedback that supports learning as it unfolds, and joint inquiry, they also give rise to concerns regarding inaccurate information, reliance on machines for thinking, academic integrity, and inequities in access. Drawing on a narrative synthesis of selected literature and institutional guidance, this conceptual paper explores the pedagogical ramifications of LLMs. The paper contends that integrating them effectively demands learning and research environments that bring together subject-specific knowledge, critical questioning, openness about bounded AI use, and demonstrable competence. Constructive alignment, self-regulated learning, cognitive load theory, and cognitive engagement supply the conceptual bases for linking intended learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities, and assessment. A cyclical process is put forward, comprising independent engagement, AI-assisted interaction under guidance, verification, application, and reflection. The paper goes on to elaborate dimensions of institutional policy, encompassing governance, curriculum, assessment, research integrity, privacy, intellectual property, equity, procurement, and quality assurance. Specific consideration is devoted to contexts with constrained ICT resources. The paper's conclusion is that the educational value of LLMs rests on purposeful design of specific institutional AI policy that is clear, transparent and progressive.

items.title: Capability atrophy: When AI automation erodes the dynamic capabilities it was meant to build
items.abstract: Firms adopt artificial intelligence (AI) automation to strengthen their dynamic capabilities, yet automation can also remove managers from the routines through which those capabilities are renewed. Drawing on the microfoundations of dynamic capabilities, organizational learning theory, and the automation–augmentation paradox, this conceptual paper develops the concept of capability atrophy and specifies when AI automation weakens, rather than builds, firm-level dynamic capabilities. Theory synthesis across research on skill erosion, organizational learning, and human–AI collaboration yields nine propositions, together with a multilevel, multi-wave mixed-methods design that uses behavioral and system-discontinuance measures to test them. The propositions hold that automation intensity relates to dynamic capability change in an inverted-U pattern, turning negative beyond a substitution threshold. Erosion travels through reduced experiential engagement, weaker skill retention, and poorer reliance calibration, and it becomes organizational when tacit knowledge is concentrated and apprenticeship paths close. Retained decision roles, frequent exceptions, and task variety are proposed to raise the threshold, whereas analytics capability alone is not. The paper places capability atrophy within existing skill-erosion research and adds a firm-level, conditional account with explicit falsification criteria. For practice, it implies that managers should track override rates, unaided diagnosis time, and other observable indicators of capability retention alongside the returns on AI investment.

items.title: Challenges of Certifying Machine Learning Trustworthiness in High-Consequence Domains
items.abstract: Machine learning (ML) systems increasingly operate in high-consequence applications where trustworthiness assessment is critical, yet stakeholders often lack the information necessary to appropriately calibrate their trust in these systems. We argue that the challenge of assessing ML trustworthiness is fundamentally one of information asymmetries that exist between developers and stakeholders, and between complex models and all human actors, including their creators. These information gaps systematically impair trust development, leading to either over-trust or under-trust in ML systems. This paper advances three claims: first, that information asymmetries fundamentally impair appropriate trust development in ML systems; second, that systematic assessment and certification processes can reduce these asymmetries by creating standardized vocabularies and evaluation procedures; and third, that organizational maturity practices directly enhance trustworthiness rather than merely signaling it. We survey existing approaches to ML trustworthiness, identify critical obstacles to effective certification, and analyze methods for reducing information asymmetries through techniques such as intelligibility and provenance metadata.

items.title: Coaching and Inclusive Lifelong Learning within an AI-Supported Skilling System
items.abstract: This paper first explains how skilling systems improve workers' and firms' capacity to adapt to changing labour markets by helping them develop adequate skills, measure progress, and reward practice in distinct tasks. Coaching within skilling systems supports managers and employees in improving performance, managing workplace challenges and transitions, pursuing life goals, and developing leadership skills. Lifelong learning helps employees and employers remain successful within their own job and generally in the labour market. Inclusive lifelong learning within a skilling ecosystem ensures that continuous education, upskilling, and reskilling opportunities reach all people regardless of background, age, or employment status. AI-supported skilling systems, like those described in this paper, use artificial intelligence (AI) to improve coaching and lifelong learning by delivering personalized coaching and removing traditional barriers to education. This also helps to identify skill gaps and adapt educational content. Multilingual translations and real-time language conversions using AI make training more inclusive and available to marginalized groups and those with basic skill gaps. AI-based chatbots and mentors support "learning in the flow of work," continuous coaching and mentoring. AI can identify industry trends, and upskilling or reskilling programs can align with existing needs. Inclusive skilling ecosystems, which are also described in the paper, use artificial intelligence to support learning, job training, and career growth fairly and are open to all people.

items.title: Compensatory Resilience and Crisis Management: When Informal Practices Substitute for Formal Systems. A Qualitative Study of Tunisian Organizations (2011–2025)
items.abstract: RésuméObjectif. Cet article identifie et hiérarchise les facteurs de résilience organisationnelle mobilisés par des organisations tunisiennes durant la décennie de crises 2011-2025 (révolution, crises sécuritaires, pandémie de COVID-19, tensions sociales, technologiques et environnementales), et analyse l’articulation entre dispositifs formels et pratiques informelles. Problématique. La littérature conçoit la résilience comme une capacité d’anticipation, de réaction et d’adaptation, mais elle documente surtout des organisations dotées de dispositifs formels de gestion de crise stabilisés ; on sait moins ce qui fonde la résilience lorsque ces dispositifs sont lacunaires, centralisés ou privés de ressources, dans un contexte d’instabilité institutionnelle durable. Cadre théorique. Nous mobilisons quatre cadres complémentaires : la résilience comme capacité, la construction collective du sens, les pratiques réelles et le bricolage, et l’apprentissage organisationnel. Approche méthodologique. Dans une posture interprétativiste et un raisonnement abductif, nous menons une enquête qualitative exploratoire par entretiens semi-directifs, analysés sous NVivo 20 par une analyse thématique hybride, déductive et inductive. Vingt responsables de la gestion de crise, choisis par échantillonnage raisonné à diversification maximale, ont été interrogés dans vingt organisations issues de dix secteurs d’activité (treize publiques ou parapubliques et sept privées). Résultats. Organisés selon les étapes de la gestion de crise (détecter, gouverner, piloter, apprendre), les résultats sont synthétisés en une classification de quatre catégories de facteurs (structurants, compensatoires, dynamiques, contextuels), traversées par deux facteurs transversaux : le facteur humain et la tension entre dispositifs formels et pratiques informelles. L’étude propose une lecture compensatoire de la résilience, formule huit propositions destinées à être testées et met en évidence des régimes de crise chronique et une dimension symbolique de la résilience. This article identifies and ranks the organizational resilience factors that Tunisian organizations drew on during the decade of crises from 2011 to 2025 (the revolution, security crises, the COVID-19 pandemic, and social, technological and environmental tensions), and examines how formal systems and informal practices interact. Research problem. The literature conceives of resilience as a capability to anticipate, respond and adapt, yet it mostly documents organizations with stabilized formal crisis-management systems; far less is known about what sustains resilience when such systems are incomplete, centralized or under-resourced, in a context of lasting institutional instability. Theoretical framework. We draw on four complementary perspectives: resilience as a capability, collective sensemaking, actual practices and bricolage, and organizational learning. Methodology. items.title: CONTROLLING AUTONOMOUS AI AGENTS : A Comparative Survey of Runtime Enforcement, Agent Architecture, Multi-Agent Monitoring and Collective Behaviour Detection
items.abstract: The rapid development of autonomous artificial intelligence agents raises a fundamental architectural question: How can human authority be preserved when AI systems increasingly plan, select, execute and adapt their own operational activities? Research addressing this challenge is developing across several distinct areas: runtime authorization, least-privilege access control, execution isolation, formal policy verification, system observability, anomaly detection and multi-agent coordination monitoring. This survey examines representative initiatives in these areas, with particular attention to thedistinction between controlling individual agent actions and identifying collective behaviour emerging through interactions among multiple agents. Nine principal research initiatives are examined: Faramesh, Tether, AgentGuardian,MCP-Secure, IsolateGPT, ACE, SentinelAgent, LumiMAS and Parity Swarm. A separate published systematic review of 58 primary studies is also considered asbackground evidence concerning the distribution of runtime-enforcement research. The survey then examines the ST-T1024 A1–A16 architecture and its complementary A17proposal for detecting emergent collective behaviour. The objective is not to establish the superiority of one architecture. It is to identify existingcontributions, examine their respective boundaries, expose unresolved research questions and establish a basis for independent technical comparison and experimentation. items.title: Designing AI for Learning, Not Answers: Learner Perceptions of Pedagogically Designed AI Interaction
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools become increasingly associated with rapid answer generation and task completion, students may come to rely on them for their speed, convenience, and immediacy. These expectations can create tensions for pedagogically designed AI agents that are intended to support guided reasoning and reflective learning rather than provide direct answers. However, limited research has examined how students perceive pedagogically designed AI agents within an authentic higher education environment. This study examined students’ perceptions of pedagogically designed GenAI agents implemented in an undergraduate auditing module at a Singapore higher education institution. Using a pre- and post-intervention survey design involving 49 final-year students, the findings indicate that although students recognised the educational value of the agents, their evaluations remained shaped by efficiency-oriented expectations associated with general-purpose large language models (LLMs). This study contributes to discussions on pedagogical AI design by highlighting tensions between efficiency and productive struggle in AI-supported learning.

items.title: Desktop review of Australian surveillance coverage of active and micromobility users
items.abstract: Background Active and micromobility transport modes, including bike riding, e-bikes, e-scooters and walking, are growing in popularity across Australia. As mode share grows, understanding their road safety profile becomes crucial. However, the extent to which Australia’s existing data infrastructure supports such surveillance has not been systematically examined. Methods We conducted a structured desktop review of Australian data sources relevant to injury, crash and exposure surveillance of active and micromobility users. Google-based searches, informed by published frameworks were conducted in August 2025. Sources underwent data extraction to capture scope, geographic and temporal coverage, coding systems, and mode-specific coverage. Results Ninety-seven data sources were identified: 41 injury sources, 13 police-collected or government-collated crash sources, 11 sources containing both crash and injury data, and 32 exposure sources. No ambulance, emergency department, or primary care source could reliably identify injured active or micromobility users from structured data fields. Hospital and deaths data could systematically identify pedestrians and pedal cyclists. Only Queensland and Tasmania could identify e-scooters in police crash data, and no jurisdiction differentiated e-bikes from pedal bicycles. Of the 15 travel surveys, only two included e-scooters as a distinct mode. Discussion National coverage of crash and injury data in Australia is constrained by inconsistent reporting, variability in crash severity definitions, and jurisdictional differences impacting on data collection (including differing regulation and implementation timeframes). Investment in non-police crash reporting mechanisms, agreement on crash severity definitions, enhanced ambulance and emergency department coding practices, and linkage between existing datasets is critical.

items.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the clinical effectiveness and alert performance of artificial intelligence-enabled clinical decision support systems in medication-related healthcare. Seven studies were included, comprising four comparative clinical evaluations and three primarily alert-performance evaluations. The review examines medication-error reduction, clinical alert validity and clinician response using outcome-specific quantitative synthesis. The original literature screening, eligibility assessment and initial data extraction were undertaken by the lead investigator. The research team was subsequently expanded to five authors during manuscript preparation and verification. The project maintains a transparent record of its protocol, methodological decisions, evidence extraction, statistical analyses and subsequent amendments. The protocol was documented retrospectively and was not prospectively registered. Target journal: International Journal of Medical Informatics.

items.title: Do LLM Agents Compromise Like Humans? Risk and Responsibility in Dyadic Decision-Making
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they must collaborate to make joint decisions. We investigate how this collaboration unfolds under risk, asking whether agents adjust their choices to accommodate their partners, how they assign responsibility for shared outcomes, and whether responsibility attribution shapes subsequent adjustment. We designed a series of agents with systematically varying risk preferences and paired them in a repeated joint decision-making task previously conducted with humans. Like humans, agents converged toward their partners' choices. However, similar aggregate behavior arose from different dynamics: agents showed little evidence of reciprocal adjustment, tended to weigh rewards more, and their responsibility attribution was decoupled from compromise. Similarly, while they showed bias in their responsibility attribution, the outcome's valence shaped the attribution differently than in humans. Our results reveal important differences between human--human and agent--agent joint decision-making, demonstrating that similar social outcomes can emerge from different social dynamics and reasoning.

items.title: Do You Even Know What I Want? Improving LLMs Ability to Detect Hidden User Intent
items.abstract: As with conventional AI agents, a common source of misalignment between Large Language Models (LLMs) and their human users is misspecified goals. Often, this happens when the human has skewed beliefs about the system's model and provides it with information that causes behavior different from what they expected, with potentially unwanted side effects. To ensure goal alignment, one solution would be for the LLM to ask the human questions about their objectives. However, it has been well-documented that LLMs most often provide default responses to user requests rather than try and ask questions to clarify their true intent. In this paper, we address these challenges by adapting a novel formulation for the objective misspecification problem to work with LLMs. We then test if LLMs that are prompted to ask questions about a user's true underlying objectives are better at identifying them compared to those that do not. We evaluate our method using four state-of-the-art LLMs tested on five standard IPC domains, showing that for some domains, asking questions greatly improved model performance.

items.title: DTAL : THE DETERMINISTIC TRANSACTION AUTHORIZATION LAYER. Paper 1: The Necessity, Threat Environment and Operating Principles of Autonomous Transaction Authorization in Agentic AI Systems
items.abstract: The rapid development of autonomous artificial intelligence agents introduces acybersecurity challenge that extends beyond the protection of conventional informationsystems. AI agents can independently plan tasks, invoke tools, communicate with external services, access data and initiate operations. When multiple agents interact, their combinedactivity may also produce collective behaviour that was not explicitly specified by theirindividual operating instructions. Traditional cybersecurity controls remain essential. However, an organisation deployingautonomous agents needs an additional architectural answer to a fundamental question: Who has the final authority to authorize an external transaction initiated by thecompany's AI ecosystem? This paper proposes the Deterministic Transaction Authorization Layer (DTAL) as theexclusive authorization authority for such interactions. DTAL is designed to integrate with the ST-T1024 deterministic AI architecture and its agentic extensions A0–A16. It also incorporates A17, a research proposal for detecting emergent collective behaviour in multi-agent systems. Under the proposed arrangement, the company's AI agents operate autonomously within defined boundaries. DTAL independently evaluates and authorizes or refuses consequential external transactions according to policies established by the company. Individual human approval is not required for routine transactions. Authorization must operate at machine speed. The architecture also proposes duplicated DTAL supervision for continuity, with the CEO and CFO holding the two human governance keys for exceptional changes to the authorization authority. This paper establishes the threat environment, rationale and operating principles. items.title: Explainable AI for Fair and Transparent Human Resource Decision- Making
items.abstract: Human resource (HR) decisions are currently supported by algorithmic processes for hiring, promotions, and retaining employees, the lack of transparency in these models raises concerns about fairness, accountability, and trust of employees towards the process. In this paper, we develop a two-channel explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model that combines the post hoc explanation methods such as SHAP and LIME with the inherently interpretable classifier for HR decisions. In our methodology, adversarial debiasing is used in the training process to prevent the influence of sensitive attributes on the model performance. For testing the effectiveness of the proposed XAI model, we conduct an experimental evaluation using IBM HR analytics dataset with three HR decision making tasks including promotion prediction, attrition prediction, and candidate selection task. As results, we show that our model achieves reductions in demographic parity disparity without compromising the explanation quality using local accuracy and stability measures. Comparing with baseline models in terms of fairness-utility trade-off consistently yields improvements.

items.title: Exploring Cognitive Synergy Framework on Computing Students Epistemic Agency in Robotics Education
items.abstract: Generative AI can support robotics programming, but students must still evaluate suggestions and justify design decisions. This study examined changes in grit-related learning dispositions and patterns of epistemic activity during instruction using the Cognitive Synergy Framework (CSF). In a mixed-methods study across six West African universities, we randomly allocated 410 undergraduates to CSF-supported or comparison instruction. A categorical-time mixed-effects model analysed 848 Grit in Robotics Programming scores from 351 students across Weeks 11, 13, and 15. Epistemic network analysis examined coded actions from 30 collaborative groups. The reported GRP condition-by-time interaction was significant, Wald χ 2 (2) = 15.02, p < .001. Relative to Week 11, estimated gains were 0.167 points greater under CSF at Week 13 (95% CI [0.059, 0.274]) and 0.213 points greater at Week 15 (95% CI [0.093, 0.333]). With a 0.20-point downward adjustment to imputed CSF scores at both follow-ups, the joint test yielded p = .103. Group-level network trajectories differed by condition (β = 0.09, 95% CI [0.03, 0.15], p = .004). Gains in independent epistemic agency remained untested. Future studies should match instructional support across conditions and assess individual reasoning, evaluative judgement, and knowledge construction on tasks completed without scaffolding.

items.title: From app open to app close: Function and well-being across TikTok sessions
items.abstract: Social media use is often measured in aggregate or characterised by a single motivation, despite individual sessions being temporally bound and potentially dynamic. We used experience sampling to capture behavioural function (entertainment, access, social attention, escape/avoidance) and momentary well-being at both the onset and offset of naturally occurring TikTok sessions. Across seven consecutive days, 161 participants produced 3,949 paired sessions. Forty-two percent of sessions ended with a different function than they began, with transitions frequently ending in entertainment. Momentary well-being changed little across sessions. In preregistered multilevel analyses, escape-oriented sessions were not reliably associated with lower post-session well-being within persons, although a small within-person association emerged when escape was defined by the function reported at session onset alone. Participants who used TikTok more often for escape also reported lower post-session well-being under the preregistered specification, but this association was attenuated in sensitivity analyses. Well-being change was more closely aligned with the function reported at session close than at session onset, although closing function and post-session well-being were assessed in the same prompt. Together, these findings show that reported function frequently differs across the boundaries of a single social media session and demonstrate the value of aligning intensive measurement with the natural boundaries of app use.

items.title: From competency lists to situation awareness-based evaluation for safe remote navigation in autonomous shipping
items.abstract: Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) are reshaping maritime work by relocating safety-critical navigation from ship bridges to Remote Operations Centres (ROCs). This review examines whether research on MASS and ROC operator skills and competencies provides a sufficient basis for assessing their application during remote navigation. A combined bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review identified peer-reviewed studies from Web of Science, Scopus, and Transport Research International Documentation (TRID), with 48 studies included in the qualitative synthesis. The bibliometric analysis shows a fragmented field in which safety and navigation are prominent, while human-element and situation-awareness themes remain less consolidated. The thematic synthesis identified five competency domains: safety-critical cognition, digital-technical and Human–Machine Interface (HMI)-related competencies, reconfigured maritime operational expertise, communication and teamwork in distributed operations, and meta-competencies and adaptive capacity. These domains were interpreted through Endsley’s three-level Situation Awareness (SA) framework to examine how competencies may support perception, comprehension, and projection before decision-making and task execution. Although studies identify many competencies required for ROC operators, they provide much less evidence on how those competencies should be evaluated during safety-critical ROC performance. Future research should examine competency–SA relationships through task- and simulator-based assessment before assuming direct transfer or inadequacy of existing maritime competencies.

items.title: From immersion to educational world-making: applying secondary world theory to AI-supported XR design in teacher education
items.abstract: Extended Reality (XR) research in education has focused on immersion, presence, engagement, simulation and experiential learning. These perspectives explain immersive learning but do not fully account for the quality of the worlds learners enter. A virtual environment may be visually compelling while remaining pedagogically shallow, weakly structured or ethically unexamined. This study develops and applies an educational adaptation of Secondary World theory to examine AI-supported XR design in teacher education. The study draws on a theory-driven secondary mixed-methods analysis of an intervention involving 140 pre-service teachers working in 24 teams. Participants designed 48 virtual environments across CoSpaces and Minecraft, using ChatGPT for scenarios, learner personas and critique, and Spline for three-dimensional assets. The analysis examined team-level design artefacts, peer feedback, coded records and reflections across seven dimensions: coherence, depth, actionability, consequence, sub-creation, transfer and reflexivity. Four levels of educational world-making were identified: scenic immersion, task-world construction, pedagogical world construction and reflexive Secondary World-making. Most designs remained scenic or task-oriented, while fewer formed coherent pedagogical worlds integrating learner roles, actions, feedback and transfer. CoSpaces tended to support structured sequencing, while Minecraft supported spatial extension and collaborative construction. These patterns reflected platform affordances and design sequence. Generative AI was most strongly associated with higher-level world-making when used to test assumptions, accessibility, learner agency and pedagogical coherence rather than generate content. The study contributes a framework for evaluating XR learning environments beyond immersion and argues that teacher education should prepare future teachers to design, evaluate and critique the educational worlds technology makes possible.

items.title: From Learner Agency to Comparable Opportunities
items.abstract: This conceptual paper traces the connection between Jean-Pol Martin’s Learning by Teaching (Lernen durch Lehren, LdL) and the New Human Rights (Neue Menschenrechte, NMR). It takes Martin’s 1985 dissertation on information processing in foreign-language teaching and his 1994 habilitation on the anthropological foundations of the curriculum as historical starting points. The paper makes explicit the normative premise that connects learner agency to institutional justice. If everyone’s basic needs deserve equal consideration, institutions should provide comparable effective opportunities to meet them. Two hypothetical examples, a classroom in which pupils take turns teaching and a municipal consultation, illustrate how access, support and influence determine whether people can meaningfully participate. The supplementary file Der Organismus als Ausgangspunkt contains the German translation of the AI-generated reconstruction by Le Chat that prompted this paper. The translation was prepared by ChatGPT.

items.title: From Organisational Trust to AI Adoption: Examining the Role of Perceived Fairness, Transparency, and Employee Confidence in AI-Enabled Human Resource Management
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming human resource management (HRM) through its applications in recruitment and selection, performance evaluation, employee engagement, learning and development, workforce planning, and talent management. Despite the operational benefits of AI-enabled HRM, employee acceptance remains influenced by concerns regarding algorithmic fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, and the reliability of automated decisions. This study develops and examines a framework explaining how perceived fairness, transparency, and employee confidence contribute to organisational trust and how organisational trust subsequently influences employees’ intention to adopt AI-enabled HRM systems. The study is conceptually grounded in organisational trust theory, organisational justice theory, and technology acceptance perspectives. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design is proposed, with an sample of 160 employees and HR professionals working in Indian organisations. A structured questionnaire based on a five-point Likert scale is used as the proposed measurement instrument. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, construct validity assessment, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression are applied to demonstrate the analysis. The findings indicate that perceived fairness, transparency, and employee confidence positively contribute to organisational trust in AI-enabled HRM. Organisational trust also demonstrates a positive association with employees’ intention to adopt AI-enabled HRM systems. The findings suggest that successful AI adoption in HRM depends not only on technological capability but also on organisational credibility, transparent decision-making, perceived procedural justice, and employee confidence. The study offers implications for Indian organisations seeking to implement responsible, trustworthy, and employee-centred AI-enabled HR practices.

items.title: From Vibe Coding to Automation, Implementation and the Cascade of Uncertainty
items.abstract: AI-native development environments are changing how digital products can be created, removing the barrier of human technical effort required to translate defined requirements into functioning software. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), this creates opportunities to participate more directly in digital production without requiring input from service providers. An appointment-based business case developed in an AI-native environment serves as one practical stress test of the implications of service design using Vibe Coding. The analysis distinguishes technical capability from economic sustainability and considers how integrated cloud services, AI computation, credit-based consumption and opaque cost attribution can complicate accountability for users with limited technical expertise. It concludes that a service provider cannot responsibly assume open-ended accountability for a system when its operating costs, dependencies and technical conditions may change beyond the provider's control. Connecting this use case to the industry's shift from Vibe Coding towards causal reasoning models and autonomous AI agents, this exploratory paper proposes quantum computing for the classification and optimisation of factory ontology data and in support of classical machine learning models. For critical manufacturing at scale, where token-based costs, energy use and sustainability goals may require it, quantum computing may provide the relevant evidence to inform and develop better tools that can intelligently manage the reliance of input by autonomous agents and black-box LLMs with that of lower expense deterministic, traditional algorithm-based logic.

items.title: Gamified Formative Assessment and Student Engagement: Measuring Cognitive and Affective Outcomes in STEM Classrooms. An Experimental Study in Imo State, South-East Nigeria
items.abstract: Gamified formative assessment, which adds game elements such as points, badges and leaderboards to low-stakes quizzes, is widely promoted as a way of increasing engagement, yet controlled evidence from sub-Saharan African STEM classrooms is scarce. This study tested the effect of gamified formative assessment on cognitive and affective outcomes among Senior Secondary 2 students in Imo State, South-East Nigeria. A pretest–posttest, delayed-posttest quasi-experimental design with a control group was used. Twelve intact Mathematics and Physics classes from 12 schools were randomly assigned to gamified assessment on digital quiz platforms (n = 158) or to non-gamified paper quizzes with the same items and feedback (n = 154) for eight weeks. After controlling for pretest scores, the gamified group outperformed the control group on the posttest, F(1, 309) = 124.13, p < .001, η²p = .29, g = 1.26, and on a delayed retention test four weeks later, F(1, 309) = 59.80, p < .001, g = 0.88. The gamified group also reported higher behavioural, emotional and cognitive engagement (g = 0.84 to 1.15) and intrinsic motivation (g = 0.84), and slightly lower test anxiety (g = −0.23). Gender did not moderate the effect. The findings suggest that gamified formative assessment can improve both achievement and engagement in resource-constrained STEM classrooms, although novelty effects and the short duration warrant caution. Keywords: Gamification; Formative Assessment; Student Engagement; Motivation; STEM Education; Nigeria

items.title: Generative AI and the Future of Work in Technology Workers' Discourse: A Topic Modelling and Clustering Analysis of Hacker News Discussions From 2023 To 2026
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the organisation of work, yet relatively little is known about how the workers closest to the technology interpret its consequences for their own occupations. This study examines how technology practitioners discuss the effects of generative AI on jobs, careers and hiring, and how this discourse changed between January 2023 and September 2026. A new corpus was assembled from Hacker News, a large online forum for software and technology professionals. Keyword retrieval was combined with a zero-shot relevance classifier, which yielded 34,270 comments written by 13,576 contributors with an estimated precision of 85.3% on a held-out random sample. Four topic models, namely LDA, NMF and two BERTopic variants, were compared on coherence, diversity and coverage, and non-negative matrix factorisation with 15 topics provided the best balance. Sentence embeddings were then clustered with k-means to identify broader discourse frames, and the monthly topic composition was segmented with contiguity-constrained hierarchical clustering to detect discourse phases. Six frames emerged, covering corporate layoffs and AI-washing, AI as a tool or a threat to the programming craft, software careers and the junior pipeline, creative and knowledge-work displacement, AI in recruitment, and macro-level automation, economy and society. Labour-related discussion intensified from about 31 to 47 comments per 1,000 AI-related comments. The only robust change point, in May 2025, marks a shift towards layoffs, careers and the entry-level pipeline and away from debates about AI in recruitment, while macro-level debate about automation remained stable. The findings indicate that practitioner attention has turned towards how employers restructure work and entry routes, with implications for human resource management, career guidance and workforce policy.

items.title: Generative AI collaboration and expatriate career adaptability: a career construction perspective on sustainable career development
items.abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) technologies become increasingly integrated into global workplaces, their implications for individual career development, particularly among internationally mobile professionals, remain underexplored. This study examines the relationship between human–GenAI collaboration and expatriates’ career adaptability, as well as three career sustainability-related outcomes: career satisfaction, life satisfaction, and perceived AI-enabled task performance. Grounded in Career Construction Theory, the study conceptualizes human–GenAI collaboration as a contextual resource associated with adaptive career responses. Drawing on data from 361 expatriates, the findings indicate that human–GenAI collaboration is positively associated with career adaptability, which in turn relates positively to these career-related outcomes. The results further show that the relationship between human–GenAI collaboration and career adaptability varies according to expatriates’ AI trust and perceived AI-induced job insecurity. This study contributes to research on career development and human–AI interaction by highlighting the role of digitally mediated work practices in adaptive career processes within global work contexts.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence-related concerns among medical students in the West Bank, Palestine: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical education. However, concerns about its professional, ethical, and psychological implications for future physicians remain insufficiently studied, particularly in resource-constrained settings. This study assessed GenAI-related concerns among Palestinian medical students in the West Bank, Palestine, using the Fear, Anxiety, Mistrust, and Ethics (FAME) scale. Methods A multi-institutional cross-sectional online survey using convenience sampling via online recruitment was conducted among medical students at Palestinian universities between March and April 2026. Data were collected on sociodemographic and academic characteristics, prior GenAI tool use, self-reported level of AI concern, and FAME scores. Non-parametric tests and multiple linear regression were used for analysis. Results Of 399 participants included in the analysis, 96.0% reported using ChatGPT. The median total FAME score was 40 (IQR, 35–45). Median domain scores were highest for Mistrust and Ethics, both with a median score of 11, compared with Fear and Anxiety, both with a median score of 9. Male students had higher Fear and Anxiety scores than female students, but total FAME scores did not differ significantly by gender. In the exploratory adjusted regression model, no sociodemographic, academic, or AI-use variable was independently associated with the total FAME score, and the overall model explained only a small proportion of score variability. Conclusions GenAI use was widespread among Palestinian medical students in the West Bank, Palestine, with higher median scores observed in the mistrust and ethics domains than in fear of professional displacement. None of the variables included in the exploratory multivariable model was independently associated with total FAME score. Structured AI-literacy education addressing ethical reasoning and critical appraisal of AI-generated information may represent a potential educational implication of these findings.

items.title: Global Trends in Generative AI Adoption: A Quantitative Survey of Postsecondary Students
items.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined reported GenAI use for academic work in 2022–23 and reported intention to use GenAI in 2023–24 among 1,021 English-fluent postsecondary students purposively recruited from multiple countries in September 2023. Descriptive statistics and exploratory, unadjusted Pearson chi-square tests examined bivariate associations with gender, primary-language category, and level-of-study category. Overall, 73.1% of participants reported using GenAI for academic work in 2022–23, and 65.6% reported intending to use it in 2023–24. Among GenAI users, 89.5% identified ChatGPT as the tool they used most. Statistically significant but small bivariate associations were found between gender and both outcomes, primary-language category and both outcomes, and graduate-versus-undergraduate category and reported use. No statistically significant association was detected between level-of-study category and reported intention. These findings provide a time-specific account of GenAI engagement within this multinational sample but do not establish population prevalence or independent demographic associations. They are compatible with selected aspects of postplagiarism, which served as an interpretive framework rather than a theory tested by the survey.

items.title: Humanity on the Threshold of Flawlessness: Defending the Right to Err in an Age of Perfect Machines
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems have begun to produce faster and less error-prone results than humans in many domains, from education and health to science and governance. This opinion paper discusses an overlooked cost of this development: error is not merely a deficiency that humans should avoid, but a constitutive experience of learning, discovery, and meaning-making. The paper distinguishes three levels, termed functional perfection, human development, and existential meaning. It argues that technology can deliver major progress at the first level but cannot by itself resolve the other two. Findings from a recent study of a community of AI agents conducting science support this claim in two ways. On the one hand, even machines improve not by eliminating error but by making it visible and correcting it. On the other hand, agents that excel in experimental rigor lag behind humans in choosing significant questions and producing original contributions. After addressing possible objections, the paper proposes implications for education, research, and policy. Its central conclusion is that the education of the future should cultivate not individuals who answer better than AI, but individuals who can ask questions beyond AI’s answers, live with uncertainty, and preserve the right to learn through error.

items.title: Humanizing the Bot: How Conversational AI Responsiveness and Perceived Anthropomorphism Mitigate Customer Decision Hesitation Through Brand Trust
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbots in e-commerce has restructured customer service delivery. However, online shoppers frequently experience pre-purchase decision hesitation due to transaction uncertainties. Grounded in Uncertainty Reduction Theory and Social Response Theory, this study investigates how Conversational AI Responsiveness and Perceived Anthropomorphism mitigate Customer Decision Hesitation through the mediating role of Brand Trust. Data were collected via an online survey from 195 e-commerce consumers in Indonesia who interacted with AI chatbots during their shopping journeys. The empirical framework was evaluated using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. The empirical results reveal that both Conversational AI Responsiveness (β=0.482,p<0.001) and Perceived Anthropomorphism (β=0.325,p<0.001) significantly foster Brand Trust, while directly and indirectly mitigating Customer Decision Hesitation. Furthermore, Brand Trust operates as a vital complementary mediating mechanism (β=-0.395,p<0.001). The structural model explains 51.4 percent of the variance in Brand Trust and 48.7 percent in Customer Decision Hesitation. This research advances Marketing Technology literature by elucidating how humanized AI interactions alleviate choice anxiety, providing strategic guidelines for digital retailers to curb cart abandonment.

items.title: I Believe in You: Robot Identity Design and Service Initiative
items.abstract: Some public-service tasks involve requests for personal information, making a robot's presented role and service behavior relevant to users’ privacy perceptions. We examine professional identity cues and service proactivity in a simulated Chinese government-service setting. Semi-structured interviews (\(n=17\)) informed the study design; a pilot study (\(n=34\)) checked the manipulations; and a 2×2 within-subjects virtual study (\(n=36\)) measured self-reported privacy sensitivity and the depth of simulated disclosure. In the main study, participants reported lower privacy sensitivity with robots presented as having a professional identity, and service proactivity interacted with identity presentation. Interviewees differed in their preferences: some found passive service less intrusive, whereas others valued proactive assistance for anticipating their needs. These findings concern perceptions and choices in a simulation, not the robot's actual institutional authorization or data security. They inform context-sensitive interaction design without treating increased disclosure as a goal or professional appearance as proof of privacy protection.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Students’ Academic Cost Reduction: A Comparative Analysis of Cost and Gender for Public Sector Universities in Hazara Division.
items.abstract: Despite the rapidly growing popularity of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in universities, this study explores its impact on students’ academic costs at the higher education level. The study focuses on higher education students at public sector universities in the Hazara Division regarding the use of AI tools to minimise their educational costs. The study used quantitative data analysis and techniques in SPSS-26. It checked the reliability and validity of the data and then used regression analysis to meet the study objectives. Findings showed that effective utilisation of AI tools positively impacts students’ overall academic costs. Strategic integration of AI tools significantly contributes to lower academic costs, as shown in the gender-based analysis.

items.title: Impact of Perceived AI Threat on Unemployment Anxiety and Psychological Well-Being among IT Employees
items.abstract: This research seeks to analyze the connection between perceived AI menace, fear of unemployment, and mental well-being of employees through a quantitative correlational approach. The emergence of artificial intelligence in the working environment raises worries in regard to job security and the threat of unemployment. Thus, there may be a rise in employment worries and a decrease in employees' mental well-being. The methodology to collect data on employees levels of perceived AI menace, fear of unemployment, and mental well-being is based on surveying them using conventional self-reported questionnaires. Descriptive statistics will be used to analyze the levels of these factors in terms of their means (M) and standard deviations (SD). The reliability analysis is going to be done for checking internal reliability of a research tool using Cronbach's alpha. To measure the relationships between these three variables, a Pearson product-moment correlation will be used. Additionally, a simple linear regression will be run in order to see if perceived threat from AI can predict unemployment anxiety and psychological well-being and if unemployment anxiety can predict psychological well-being. The measurement of psychological well-being is going to be based on the six dimensions introduced by Ryff: autonomy, environmental mastery, personal growth, positive relations with others, purpose in life, and self-acceptance. The results of this study will allow understanding how the way employees view AI being a threat to their jobs relates to worries about unemployment and psychological well-being. All in all, the results of this research can be helpful for realizing the significance of recognizing employees’ concerns in the course of technological changes and encourage businesses to provide adequate support to employees for mitigating job-related uncertainty and reaching psychological well-being.
